nameStory: This beetle gets its straightforward name from its favorite food - viburnum shrubs, whose leaves it devours with gusto. The larvae and adults both feast exclusively on these popular landscaping plants, making them easy to spot munching away on viburnum foliage throughout the growing season.
description: The viburnum leaf beetle is a small, brownish leaf beetle that specializes in eating viburnum shrubs. Adults are about the size of a ladybug, with a somewhat elongated oval shape and tan to brown coloring. This European native has become a serious pest in New England since its arrival, capable of completely defoliating viburnum plants when populations are high. Both the adults and their yellow, spiny larvae can cause significant damage to ornamental and native viburnums.

idTips.label: Host plant specificity
idTips.description: Always found on viburnum shrubs - if you see small beetles or spiny yellow larvae eating viburnum leaves, you've likely found them

idTips.label: Adult appearance
idTips.description: Small brownish beetles about 4-6mm long with an elongated oval shape, similar size to a ladybug but more muted in color

idTips.label: Larval stage
idTips.description: Yellow-green larvae with black spots and spiny projections that feel slightly bristly to touch, found in groups on leaf undersides

idTips.label: Feeding damage
idTips.description: Creates distinctive skeletonized leaves where only the leaf veins remain, giving damaged foliage a lacy, see-through appearance

idTips.label: Egg sites
idTips.description: Small holes in viburnum twigs where eggs were laid, often visible as tiny dark spots or slightly swollen areas on young branches

habitat: Found wherever viburnum shrubs grow in New England, from suburban gardens and parks to woodland edges where native viburnums thrive. Common in residential landscapes, botanical gardens, and naturalized areas with arrowwood viburnum and other native species. Shows up at all elevations where suitable host plants are present.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering sites and begin laying eggs in viburnum twigs. Look for small brownish beetles on newly emerging viburnum leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with yellow spiny larvae feeding heavily on leaves, creating the characteristic skeletonized damage. Adults are also present and feeding.
seasonality.fall: New generation of adults emerges and feeds before seeking overwintering sites. Egg-laying for next year's generation occurs in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter and bark crevices near viburnum plants. Look for old egg-laying holes as dark spots on bare viburnum twigs.

funFact: This beetle was crowned the "number one pest species" by UK gardeners in 2010, beating out slugs, aphids, and all other garden villains for the title of most troublesome bug!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small brown beetles, but its exclusive presence on viburnum plants is the dead giveaway - remember "viburnum beetle, viburnum only" and you'll never mix it up with other leaf beetles that eat different plants.
contextualKnowledge: This invasive species was actually first collected in North America way back in 1924 in Nova Scotia, but wasn't recognized as established until much later. It highlights how non-native insects can quietly build populations for decades before becoming obvious problems.
compareHints: This is the only Pyrrhalta species commonly found in New England, making identification easier than with many beetle groups. It can be distinguished from other leaf beetles in the Chrysomelidae family by its exclusive association with viburnum plants and its distinctive larval stage with prominent spines. Most other leaf beetles in our region either look quite different as adults or feed on completely different plant families.
